newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Taiwan Sep jet fuel tender offers at $191-$192.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Sep jet fuel tender offers at $191-$192.

text.p: Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) have attracted lower offers in its jet fuel import tender for September delivery compared with the previous tender for August, traders said on Thursday.
They said the offers ranged between $191 and $192 per tonne, compared with around $197 per tonne in its last tender for August 1-10 delivery, on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) basis.
CPC sources said the latest tender for 32,000 tonnes of jet fuel attracted between 12 and 15 offers.
But they said CPC might not award the tender, which closed on July 30, as most of the offers were for first half September delivery.

One CPC source said while the tender had sought a cargo for September 1-20 delivery, the company's marketing and refining departments have requested for cargoes to be delivered during the second half of September.

"They wanted to delay the delivery because inventories are higher than expected," the source said. "It might not even be necessary to import for September, that's why they want it to be delivered later."
The source said a decision will be made on Friday either to accept the first-half September cargoes offered, or to cancel and re-issue the tender.
Traders said some sellers would be willing to offer second-half September cargoes instead but at a higher price of around $195 per tonne, c-and-f basis.
One trader said even the $195-level is a good offer in a contango market, which translates to a 50-to-60-cent-per-barrel discount to the Singapore swaps values, free-on-board basis.
The CPC source also said the delay has nothing to do with the recent record fall in the Taiwanese dollar and that the country will not reduce its oil product imports.
The Taiwan dollar plunged to its lowest level against the U.S. dollar since 1988 to close on Thursday at its intraday low of T$28.70 to the dollar against Wednesday's T$28.480 finish.
Some analysts said it could test T$29.00.
"The country's total imports might be reviewed but the reduction will not be on oil products because energy is needed everyday," the source said.
"The lower exchange rate will certainly increase CPC's costs but CPC is still a monopoly and if costs rose, we are flexible to change local prices to cover them."
